en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk 14.
The Training Rule on the Six Years.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the monks were having blankets made every year.
They lived occupied with much begging and much requesting, saying:
"Give us wool!"
“There is need for rams’ wool,” they said.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, have rugs made every year? They will live full of begging and full of requests!”
“Give us wool; we have need of wool.
“But our own rugs, once made, last us five or six years, during which our children urinate upon them, spit upon them, and are even eaten by rats.
Yet these recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, have rugs made for them every year, living full of begging and full of requests.”
“‘Give us sheep’s wool; we have need of sheep’s wool.
The bhikkhus heard those people complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... they complained, grumbled, and lamented:
“How can these monks have blankets made every year, living with such abundance of begging and such abundance of requests, saying:
‘Give us wool; we need wool’?
Then those monks, having rebuked them in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. …pe…
“Is it true, monks, that the monks have woolen blankets made every year, and live full of requests and full of entreaties, saying:
‘Give us wool; we need wool’?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can those foolish men, monks, have blankets made every year, living full of requests and full of entreaties, saying:
‘Give us wool! We need wool!’?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the inspiration of those without faith...
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘When a monk has had a new rug made, it should be kept for six years.’”
“If, after six years, a monk should have another new rug made—whether he has disposed of the old one or not—he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, a certain monk was ill in Kosambī.
His relatives sent a messenger to that bhikkhu, saying, "May the venerable sir come; we shall attend upon him.
The bhikkhus also spoke thus:
“Go, friend; your relatives will attend to you.
He replied:
“Friends, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One—”
“Furthermore, it has been said: ‘A monk who has had a new rug made must keep it for six years.
Now I am ill and am unable to depart taking my rug with me;
moreover, without my rug, I find no comfort.”
“I will not go,” they said.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on that occasion and in that connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, to grant the authorization for a rug to a sick monk.
And this, monks, is how it should be granted:

That sick monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the elder monks, having sat down on his heels and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak as follows:”
‘Venerable sir,
I am ill and am unable to depart taking my rug with me. Therefore,
venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha for authorization regarding the rug.’
A second time she should be asked;
a third time she should be asked.
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk named so-and-so is ill and is unable to depart taking his rug with him.
He requests from the Saṅgha authorization for his rug.’
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant formal authorization for a rug to the bhikkhu named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.
This monk named so-and-so is ill and is unable to depart taking his rug with him.
He requests formal authorization from the Sangha for his rug.
The Sangha grants formal authorization for the rug to the monk named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of granting the authorization for a rug to the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The authorization for a rug has been granted by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so.
“It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent.
Thus do I understand this.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“Furthermore, having had a new rug made, a monk must use it for six years.

If, before the end of those six years, he should have another new rug made—whether he has disposed of the former rug or not—except with the consent of the monks, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Regarding the term “new”:
It is called "made" by way of the instrument.
That which is called "spread" (saṇṭhataṃ) is that which has been made by spreading it out, not woven.
"Having had it made" means either having made it oneself or having had it made by another.
"It should be worn for six years."
It should be kept for a maximum of six years.
"If within six years" means less than six years.
"Having relinquished that spread" means having given it to others.
"Without relinquishing" means...
"Having given it to no one.
"Except by the consent of the Saṅgha" means:
setting aside the consent of the Saṅgha, if one makes or causes another to make a new spread (santhatā), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of undertaking.
By the mere acquisition [of it], it becomes subject to relinquishment.
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be relinquished:
…pe… “Venerable sir, this rug of mine was made by me in less than six years, except by means of the monks’ formal authorization; it is an article to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. …pe…
"Should give," ... "should give," ... "I give to the Venerable One."
If one completes by oneself what was begun by oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
If one has others complete what was begun by oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one completes by oneself what was begun by others, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she causes what was begun by others to be completed by others, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
There is no offense if she completes it over the course of six years.
If he makes it for more than six years;
or if he makes it or causes it to be made for the sake of another;
or if, having obtained what was made by another, he uses it.
If one makes a canopy, or a floor-covering, or a screen-wall of grass-cloth, or a mattress, or a pillow,
with the consent of the monks,
or if one is insane.
"For one who is a first offender.
The fourth training rule on the six years is concluded.
